resources.title: If $dy/dx$ is inversely proportional to $x^2$, can we find $y$?
resources.evidence: Exam-register question: 'It is given that dy/dx is inversely proportional to x^2' with 'y and dy/dx are each equal to 1 when x=2' — the student writes dy/dx = c/x^2 (the DE formulated from the proportionality statement, 3.8.1 verbatim — the suggestion scaffolds exactly this step: 'Can you write this mathematically? Can we now replace a with dy/dx'), determines c from dy/dx(2)=1, integrates to the general form y = -4/x + d (3.8.2), and evaluates d from y(2)=1 (the initial condition giving the particular solution, 3.8.3). JOIN: rides its of-record pure-1-integration body (the 1.8.2 constant-of-integration reading of record, cross-map lane 8); the 1.8.2 alignment stands and the part-(ii) DE pipeline is the 3.8 embodiment (the lane-6 one-to-many law).

nonOverlapRows.title: Weight pulling
nonOverlapRows.routedTo: P3 3.8 companion disclosure (a separable DE solved with machinery beyond the spec)
nonOverlapRows.reason: Approach 1 formulates the tractrix DE dy/dx = -y/sqrt(a^2-y^2) from the string geometry and separates the variables ('This is a separable differential equation, so we get integral(sqrt(a^2-y^2)/y) dy = -x+c') with an initial condition (x=0, y=a) — the 3.8.1-3.8.3 pipeline verbatim — but the evaluation requires the substitution y = a sin(theta) and the cosecant integral, both beyond the 9709 function set, and Approach 2 leans on cosh/arcosh catenary machinery; the resource's centre of gravity is the tractrix/catenary geometry. The genuine separable-DE skeleton is disclosed by reference (the prior log/exp and trig non-overlap rows stand).
